newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel hopes for quick sale of Hapoalim.
newsitem.headline: Israel hopes for quick sale of Hapoalim.

text.p: Three years after it published its first tender for a controlling stake in Bank Hapoalim, Israeli government officials said on Tuesday they believe a second tender now in the works will lead to a quick sale.

Finance Minister Dan Meridor announced on Monday that Israel would be publishing the terms for selling a controlling holding in the bank next week. Prospective bidders will have 45 days from then to announce their intention to bid, the Treasury said.

The government, which today controls 78 percent of Israel's biggest commercial bank, will be offering to sell as little as 25 percent and up to its full holding, minus an undetermined percentage to be offered to bank employees.

As recently, as last August the prospects for a sale looked dim after the most serious bidding consortium -- a group headed by Claridge, the Israeli investment vehicle of Canadian entrepreneur Charles Bronfman -- dropped out.
Since then, officials involved in the bank sale process two new groups have emerged.
The first is headed by Ted Arison, an American entrepreneur of Israeli origin. The group includes Claridge, which its president Jonathan Kober, said would take approximately an 18 percent interest.
The second is led by U.S. banker Jeffrey Keil and includes Eliezer Fishman, a leading Israeli entrepreneur who had worked to form a group at the time of the first tender.
"There appears to be two groups....Maybe there will be others. At this stage we don't know," said one official involved in the sale.

Newspaper reports said the 45-day period for presenting applications was aimed at giving new investors to consider bids. The official denied newspaper reports there would be a $50 million deposit required of bidders.
Hapoalim is one of several banks the government acquired after it bailed out shareholders in the wake of the 1983 bank shares crash. Re-privatisation has since gone slowly.
In Hapoalim's case, the government has taken a double-barreled approach, floating shares on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange while seeking a controlling shareholder.

The Treasury published its first tender for Hapoalim in December 1994, but the sale was subject to repeated delays. Last year, parliament approved legislation forcing the banks to sell off part of their non-bank holdings as the sale was under way.
Analysts said the renewed interest in Hapoalim was due changes the political environment than in banking.
"I don't think anything has changed fundamentally with the banks that would trigger interest," said Denise Vergot-Holle, a banking analyst at Merrill Lynch in London.

"I think it was the peace process -- the agreement on Hebron," she said, adding: "The government talks more seriously about privatisation (than its predecessor). It might seem more worthwhile for the two groups to invest the time in an offer."

Matthew Czepliwicz, a banking analyst for Salomon Brothers, noted that the decline in Israeli banks' interest rate margins had bottomed out and might reverse. Vergot-Holle said the banks were stronger than any time in the recent past.
"For me, the big story is that they have cleaned up thier loan books," she said. "They've gone from being basket cases to cash cows."

She said whoever acquired Hapoalim would probably concentrate on divesting further its non-bank holdings and implementing cost-cutting measures. Because Israel is a mature banking market, she said, such measures would be the main tool for boosting earnings.
